title: Geospatial Indexing
summary: Indexing "what's near this point" efficiently — geohashing, quadtrees, and R-trees, the structures behind every proximity-search feature.

slides.markdown:
"Find every coffee shop within 2km" or "show me the 10 nearest drivers" are proximity queries — and neither a B-tree nor an [inverted index](inverted-index) is built to answer them efficiently, because both index one dimension at a time while location is inherently two-dimensional.

This topic covers the three structures built specifically for "what's near this point": geohashing, quadtrees, and R-trees. Every ride-sharing, delivery, and store-locator feature you've used is built on one of these underneath.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a normal index can't answer "find everything within 2km" efficiently
slides.markdown:
A B-tree index on latitude and a separate one on longitude each sort in one dimension. Query "within 2km of this point" and neither index alone helps: filtering by latitude range still leaves points that are far away in longitude, and vice versa — you'd need to intersect two range scans and still filter the leftover candidates by actual distance, which stops scaling once the dataset gets large or points cluster densely in one area.

The real problem is that proximity is a genuinely 2D relationship, and a 1D sorted structure discards exactly the information (how the two dimensions relate to each other) that makes "nearby" meaningful. Geospatial indexes solve this by encoding or partitioning space so nearness in the real world maps to nearness in the index.

slides.sectionTitle: Geohashing: encoding 2D coordinates into a sortable string so nearby points share a prefix
slides.markdown:
**Geohashing** encodes a (latitude, longitude) pair into a single string by recursively subdividing the world into halves — alternating latitude and longitude — and appending a bit for which half the point falls in, then converting the bit string to base32. The result is a short string like `9q8yy` where every added character narrows the represented area further.

The key property: two points that are geographically close usually share a long common prefix, since they fall into the same coarse grid cell before diverging into finer ones. That turns "find nearby points" into "find strings with a shared prefix" — a problem a normal sorted index (or even the [trie](autocomplete-and-typeahead) structure from typeahead) already knows how to solve efficiently.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a geohash grid and the edge case where two nearby points land in different cells
slides.markdown:
![Two nearby points straddling a geohash cell boundary](assets/geohash-boundary.svg)

Geohash prefix-sharing works well for points solidly inside the same cell, but two points a few meters apart can straddle a cell boundary and end up with completely different prefixes — geographically adjacent, but nowhere near each other as strings.

This is the structural trade-off of any grid-based scheme: it's fast and simple, but boundary effects are unavoidable and have to be handled explicitly, not assumed away (covered as this topic's pitfall).

slides.sectionTitle: Quadtrees: recursively subdividing space into denser cells where points are denser
slides.markdown:
A **quadtree** also recursively divides space into four quadrants, but — unlike a geohash's fixed-depth grid — it only subdivides further where points are actually dense. A quadrant with one point stays a single leaf; a quadrant packed with thousands of points keeps splitting into four smaller quadrants until each is manageably sparse.

This makes a quadtree naturally adaptive to real-world data distribution: a sparse rural area gets large, coarse cells, while a dense city center gets many small cells — the opposite of a uniform grid, which would either waste cells on empty space or leave city-center cells too crowded to search efficiently.

slides.sectionTitle: R-trees: bounding boxes that group nearby objects for fast range queries
slides.markdown:
An **R-tree** groups nearby objects into a hierarchy of rectangular **bounding boxes**: leaf nodes hold actual objects (points, or shapes like a delivery zone polygon), and each parent node's box is the smallest rectangle containing all of its children's boxes. A range query walks down from the root, only descending into child boxes that actually overlap the query area — boxes with no overlap are skipped entirely without looking at what's inside them.

R-trees handle more than points — they're the standard structure when what you're indexing has real *extent* (a building footprint, a delivery zone, a road segment), which geohashing and quadtrees, built around points, don't naturally represent.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: geohashing vs quadtree vs R-tree on query pattern and update cost
slides.markdown:
| | Geohashing | Quadtree | R-tree |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data shape | Points, fixed-depth grid | Points, adaptive to density | Points or shapes with extent |
| Nearby query | Prefix match (plus neighbor cells) | Tree traversal | Tree traversal, bounding-box overlap |
| Adapts to density | No — uniform grid regardless of data | Yes — subdivides only where dense | Yes — boxes grow/shrink to fit contents |
| Update cost | Cheap — recompute one string | Can require rebalancing on insert/delete | Can require rebalancing on insert/delete |
| Storage-friendly | Yes — plain sortable string, fits any index | Needs a tree structure | Needs a tree structure |

**How to decide:** geohashing is the simplest and fits naturally into an existing sorted index (or even a normal database column) — good default for points at moderate scale. Quadtrees shine when point density varies a lot across the space. R-trees are the right choice once you're indexing shapes with real extent, not just points — this is the structure the proximity-service pattern (matching riders to nearby drivers) typically assumes underneath.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a geohash prefix search missing a nearby point that falls just across a cell boundary
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "To find nearby points, just search for other geohashes sharing the same prefix as my query point."

**Why it's wrong:** two points can be physically meters apart but sit on opposite sides of a grid cell boundary, giving them completely different geohash prefixes from an early character onward. A naive prefix search misses these truly-nearby points entirely, silently — the query returns results, they just quietly exclude anything that happened to fall in a neighboring cell.

**Correct model:** query the target cell *and* its neighboring cells (typically the 8 surrounding cells, since a point can be near any edge or corner of its own cell), then filter the combined candidates by actual distance. This is standard practice in every real geohash-based proximity search, not an edge case to special-case later.
